A map is a drawing of all or part of the Earth's surface on a flat plane, reduced by a scale and simplified with symbols. Maps are either general (showing many features, such as a topographic map or an atlas) or thematic (showing one theme, such as rainfall or population density).

A numerical scale such as $1 : 50\,000$ means 1 unit on the map equals 50 000 of the same units on the ground. A verbal scale says it in words ("1 cm represents 500 m"), and a graphic scale is a bar, which stays correct when the map is enlarged or reduced.

In 1912 Alfred Wegener proposed that the continents had once formed one supercontinent, Pangaea, and had drifted apart. His evidence: the coasts of South America and Africa fit like a jigsaw; the same fossils (such as Mesosaurus and Glossopteris) and rock types are found on continents now oceans apart; and traces of ancient glaciers appear in places that are now tropical. In the 1960s sea-floor spreading explained the mechanism: new crust forms at mid-ocean ridges and old crust sinks back at trenches, driven by convection in the mantle.

An earthquake is a sudden shaking of the ground when stress built up in rocks is released, usually as rock slips along a fault. Most are tectonic (at plate boundaries); others are volcanic or caused by collapse, for example of caves or mines. The point underground where the rupture starts is the focus (hypocentre); the point on the surface directly above it is the epicentre.

Magnitude and intensity

Magnitude (Richter or moment magnitude) measures the energy released and is the same everywhere. Each step up means about 10 times bigger ground motion and about 32 times more energy. Intensity (the Modified Mercalli scale, I–XII) describes the shaking and damage at a particular place, so it is higher near the epicentre.

Forces from inside the Earth (endogenic) build up the land; forces at the surface (exogenic) wear it down. The exogenic processes are weathering, mass movement, erosion and deposition.

Mass movement

Mass movement is the movement of weathered material down a slope under gravity: rockfalls, landslides (a mass sliding on a slip surface), mudflows and slow soil creep (shown by tilted trees and fences). It is most likely on steep slopes, after heavy rain, where vegetation has been cleared and where earthquakes shake the ground.

Erosion and deposition

Erosion is the removal and transport of material by running water, wind, waves and glaciers. When the agent slows down it drops its load: deposition. Soil erosion by rain on bare, sloping farmland is a serious problem; it is reduced by terracing, contour ploughing, cover crops and reforestation.

Groundwater is water that fills the pores and cracks in soil and rock below the surface. Rain soaks in (infiltration) and seeps down (percolation) until it reaches the zone of saturation, where every pore is full. The top of this zone is the water table. A layer that holds and lets through plenty of water is an aquifer (sand, gravel, porous limestone); a layer that hardly lets water through, such as clay, is an aquiclude.

Pumping more groundwater than rain can refill lowers the water table and dries up wells. In clay-rich coastal cities it also makes the ground compact and sink (land subsidence): parts of north Jakarta have sunk several metres. Near the coast, sea water can seep into the aquifer (seawater intrusion), making wells salty.

Oceans cover about 71% of the Earth's surface. The science of the oceans is oceanography. Seas are classified by how they formed: transgression seas formed when rising sea level flooded low land after the ice age (shallow, such as the Java Sea); ingression seas lie in sinking parts of the crust (deep, such as the Banda Sea); and regression seas are shrinking.

⟦0⟧ ⟦1⟧

Depth zones

The sea bed is also divided by depth: the littoral zone (between high and low tide), the neritic zone (to 200 m, sunlit and rich in fish), the bathyal zone (200–2 000 m) and the abyssal zone (below 2 000 m, dark and cold).

⟦2⟧

Temperature and currents

Sea water is warmest at the surface. Below a mixed layer the temperature drops quickly through the thermocline, then stays cold (about 2–4 °C) in the deep. Ocean currents are driven by winds and by differences in temperature and salinity. Warm currents flow from the equator towards the poles, and cold currents flow towards the equator (the Humboldt current off Peru), bringing up nutrients and rich fishing grounds.

Tides are the regular rise and fall of the sea, caused mainly by the Moon's gravity and partly by the Sun's. The Moon pulls the ocean into a bulge on the side facing it, and a second bulge forms on the opposite side. As the Earth turns, most coasts pass through two bulges a day: two high tides and two low tides roughly every 24 hours 50 minutes. The difference in height between high and low tide is the tidal range.
